The 2008 financial crisis grew out of a housing bubble in the early 2000s, when home buying surged and subprime mortgages became widespread. These loans, designed for borrowers with weaker credit, carried higher interest rates and were aggressively promoted by some lenders and brokers, who profited from steering buyers into riskier products. Some borrowers took on mortgages they didn’t understand or couldn’t afford, believing they could refinance as home values rose. [...] But when the bubble burst and housing prices fell, refinancing became difficult. Defaults rose, and the losses cascaded through Wall Street. Large financial institutions had not only sold bundles of loans as mortgage-backed securities to investors, but they had also invested in them, leaving firms like Lehman Brothers exposed when the market collapsed. Turmoil spread and credit froze across the economy.

plan.title: What Really Caused the 2008 Financial Crisis
plan.description: The 2008 financial crisis told as a story: the US housing boom, subprime mortgages, securitization, the fall of Lehman Brothers and the government response. Learn how a chain of risky loans froze credit around the world.

beats.narration: On September 15, 2008, a 158-year-old Wall Street bank filed the largest bankruptcy in American history. It had survived the Great Depression. So what broke it?

props.label: Lehman Brothers' assets when it collapsed, September 15, 2008

beats.narration: The story starts earlier, in the early 2000s. Home buying surged. Prices climbed, and people believed they only went up. Houses felt like a safe bet for everyone.

clip_queries: for sale sign in front of house

beats.narration: To feed the boom, lenders pushed subprime mortgages. These were loans for borrowers with weaker credit, with higher interest rates and low teaser rates at the start.

props.definition: A home loan made to a borrower with weaker credit, carrying higher interest rates than a standard loan.

beats.narration: Many borrowers took loans they did not understand or could not afford. They figured they could refinance later, as their home value rose. Brokers profited from steering them into riskier products.

props.alt: signing loan documents at a desk

beats.narration: Why did lenders not care about risk? Because they did not keep the loans. They sold them. The three checks of collateral, credit history and character slowly disappeared.
Here is how the pipeline worked. Lenders sold loans to Wall Street. Banks bundled them into securities. Investors bought those securities, and the cash flowed back to lenders to make more loans.
Between 2005 and 2006, about 1.2 trillion dollars of subprime loans were made. Roughly 80 percent of them were securitized. The more loans they sold, the more fees lenders earned.

Banks then re-sliced these bundles into complex products called CDOs. Rating agencies stamped many of them AAA, the safest grade. Investors trusted the label, and nobody looked closely at the loans inside.

props.text: Risky loans, repackaged, wearing a AAA label.

beats.narration: Banks also borrowed heavily to buy more of them, with leverage as high as 40 to 1. And insurers like AIG sold protection against losses. The whole system leaned on one thing: rising house prices.
Then the bubble burst. Home prices fell, and refinancing became almost impossible. Defaults rose. The losses cascaded through Wall Street, because banks had kept many of these securities themselves.
Lehman Brothers was deeply exposed. It had kept the riskiest pieces of its mortgage bundles. On September 10 it announced 5.6 billion dollars in write-downs, and its stock had plunged 93 percent.

props.alt: Lehman Brothers building in New York

beats.narration: Lehman looked for a rescue. A buyout fell through. Bank of America talks broke down. The Fed refused to guarantee its loans, as it had for Bear Stearns six months earlier. Lehman filed for bankruptcy.
Credit froze. Banks stopped lending to each other, and the panic spread across the world. Lehman had 26,000 employees, and its collapse sparked chaos in markets everywhere.
Washington stepped in. Congress passed the Emergency Economic Stabilization Act, creating the Troubled Asset Relief Program, called TARP. It set aside 700 billion dollars to steady the banks.

props.label: Authorized for TARP under the 2008 stabilization act

beats.narration: So what really caused the crisis? Not one thing. Risky loans, repackaged as safe, bought with borrowed money. When prices fell, the whole chain broke. Safe-looking debt is only as strong as its weakest loan.
